sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo46/4g.xml (Pseudo-Dioscoride, Theriaca), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. Ne couvre que la partie du traite consacree aux animaux venimeux et a leurs morsures/piqures (signes cliniques puis traitements, animal par animal) ; le long prooimion methodologique initial (discussion abstraite sur la theorie des causes en medecine, sans rapport direct avec un animal precis) n'a pas ete traduit. Structure aplatie en chapitres continus a partir du decoupage interne, plus irregulier, du temoin grec source.

div.head: Signs of a rabid dog, and of those bitten by it
div.p: We have placed first, before the rest, the discussion of those bitten by a rabid animal, since the dog is a common and familiar creature, is frequently seized by rabies and destroyed by it, and is hard to guard against; and the danger from it is not to be turned aside unless one has recourse to many remedies.

The dog most often goes mad in the height of summer heat, though sometimes also in spells of cold. Once mad, it refuses both food and drink; much frothy phlegm runs from its mouth and nostrils; its look is fierce and gloomier than usual; and, without barking, it attacks and bites all alike — beasts and men, those it knows and strangers — indiscriminately. At the moment it causes no trouble beyond the pain of the wound itself; but later it produces the condition called hydrophobia. This comes on with convulsions and reddening over the whole body, especially the face, together with sweating and helplessness; some flee the light, others waste away continually; some even bark, like dogs, and bite those who approach them, and by biting become the cause of the same affliction in others. Of those who have fallen into this condition we know of none who recovered, save that we have heard by report of one or two who survived: Eudemus says that a certain man recovered, and some say that Themison, having been bitten and fallen into the condition, was saved; others say that he fell into the same state after tending a friend with hydrophobia eagerly and out of sympathy, and, after suffering greatly, recovered. The condition, then, is a grievous one; yet even before this account of it, we ourselves have saved many, and have known others saved by different physicians.

div.head: Local treatment of the bites of a rabid dog
div.p: One part of the treatment is common, to be used in the case of all who have been bitten by any venomous creature; another is peculiar to those bitten by a rabid dog, being of the greatest help to some, but unsuited to those bitten a long time before. We shall set out the special treatment first, and then run through the common one.

One must burn river-crabs upon a stick of white vine, grind their ash fine, and keep it stored away; likewise one should keep by a supply of gentian root, pounded and sifted. Whenever someone is bitten by a rabid dog, one should put into four cups of unmixed wine two spoonfuls of the crab-ash and one spoonful of the gentian, stir it as one stirs steeped barley-meal, and give it to drink from the first day up to the fourth day. This is how the remedy should be given from the start; but if two or three days have already passed since the bite before the treatment is begun, one must give three times the amount stated at first. This is the best remedy for those bitten by a rabid animal — indeed, by itself alone it has sufficed for some — and it should be used with confidence; but for the sake of further security against a danger that seems otherwise inescapable, there is nothing to prevent using the other remedies as well. It is better, if it comes to that, to endure needlessly the harshness of the remedies than, through negligence, to fall into danger.

One need not be so wary of large wounds from a rabid bite as of small ones resembling mere scratches; for through the larger wounds a great copious flow of blood can also wash out the venom along with it, but through the smaller ones this is by no means so. From the larger wounds the loosened flesh should be removed on the spot, and the edges pared away with a sharp blade; and once the flesh has been drawn up with a hook or probe, the excision should be completed. In both cases the surrounding area should be scarified with rather deep cuts, so that the greater loss of blood may counteract the spreading of the venom through the body. A cupping-glass applied with much flame can also give great benefit, so as to loosen the force of the venom.

Cauterization is the most effective remedy of all for venomous bites, for fire, being stronger than any other force, at once holds the venom in check and prevents it from being carried further inward, and at the same time the checked portion of it lays no ordinary foundation for the treatment that follows, since the ulceration is thereby kept open longer. One must take special care over the falling away of the scab, so that the wound may not close up too quickly. Rather, if possible, the ulcerations should be kept open, inflamed and irritated, well past the usual time; and this effect will be produced by applying salted preserved fish, wild garlic finely ground, and onions likewise; the best gum-resin for this is the Cyrenaic kind, or the one called Median or Parthian. Grains of wheat should be applied, both chewed and unchewed; for when softened by the moistening they widen the wounds. Some think that the chewed grains have a certain sympathetic virtue derived from the fasting of those who chewed them, though this is not certain; still, they may be used as occasion allows. And if, as often happens, the scars close over before the proper time, they should be opened again by hand, stripping away the flesh and cutting, or even cauterizing again, as the case allows; but once the appointed time has passed, the wounds should be allowed to heal over, the whole area being covered with a salt plaster, and after a few days a mustard plaster applied.

div.head: On the diet of those bitten by a rabid dog, and on the course of the affliction
div.p: Such, then, is the local treatment of those bitten by a rabid dog. One must also aim the diet against the venom, so that it may at once blunt and quench its force, and prevent it from being carried deeper; for what is thus checked resists the further penetration of the destructive power. Both of these effects can be produced by drinking rather strong unmixed wine, sweet wine, and milk; for those who take all these as part of their regimen offer some resistance to the venom, since the wine wears away all its sharpness. Likewise the eating of garlic, leeks, and onions has the same effect, for these too are altogether hard to alter and slow to lose their properties, their qualities persisting for many days when not overcome or transformed by the destructive force; and it is by their contrary qualities that they are able to master it. For this purpose there is also need of antidotes — the theriac, the one called Eupatorium, the Mithridatic, and every other kind compounded from a great many spices, for all spices, by their composition, are hard to alter in their powers and substance; hence they are able to hold their own within the body. Such, then, is the manner of diet.

One should know that the onset of the hydrophobic affliction has no fixed limit of time; for although it most often occurs within forty days, in those who have neglected themselves it has sometimes come on after six months, and even after a year — this we ourselves have seen — and some report that in certain cases it does not set in until after seven years. Such, then, is the treatment in the early stages of those bitten by a rabid animal. But if, for whatever reason, the aforesaid remedies are not applied in the first days, one must give up stripping away the flesh and cauterizing, for these can no longer reach deeply enough to have effect; there is no benefit from applying them then, and the body would be needlessly subjected to pain. A different course of treatment should instead be followed: purging, which can be of great benefit, since by moving the body it helps to alter its whole condition — the sacred remedy through colocynth; and also split goat’s milk, which can provide both purging and tempering; sharp, pungent foods and the drinking of unmixed wine should also be taken daily, being able to blunt the venom; and besides these, the inducing of sweat both before and after food; and plucking and mustard-plastering applied part by part over the whole body. Of all these the most effective by far is known to be the administration of hellebore, and this remedy should be used with confidence — not once, nor twice, but many times, both before the fortieth day and after; for the remedy carries such power that of those already showing the first symptoms of hydrophobia, some have been saved by taking hellebore at the very first onset of the symptom. But for those already fully seized by the affliction, not even hellebore itself is able to save them.

We have set out first the treatment of those bitten by a rabid animal, for the reason stated above. Passing now to the rest of the venomous creatures, we shall first set out their several signs under a single heading; after this, the common treatment suited to all alike; and following that, we shall show whether any remedy is by nature especially helpful for particular cases; and we shall likewise note those that are altogether beyond help.

div.head: On the phalangium (spider)
div.p: In those bitten by phalangia, the place itself is reddened and resembles a puncture, neither swollen nor unusually hot, but only moderately reddish, and, on the contrary, cold to the touch. There follows trembling through the whole body, and tension about the groin and the hollows of the knees resembling spasm; pain about the loins, and a continual irritation urging one to urinate; great difficulty in the passing of the excrement; likewise a cold sweat is given off over the whole surface of the body; the eyes water and are somewhat dimmed.

div.head: On the scolopendra (centipede)
div.p: In those bitten by the creature called the scolopendra, or the ‘snake-comb,’ the area around the bite turns livid and putrefies; sometimes, though rarely, it appears wine-dark and reddish. Beginning from the bite itself, an ulceration forms — a painful one, and slow to heal; and besides this, an itching sensation spreads over the whole body.

div.head: On the scorpion
div.p: In those stung by a scorpion, the place immediately begins to inflame, becoming hard, reddened, and tightly stretched, with pain; and by turns, now a burning heat takes hold, now a chill; a sudden pain comes on, at times easing, at times growing more intense. There follow sweating and a shivering sensation, trembling and a chilling of the extremities, swelling of the groin, and flatulence passed through the rectum; the hair stands on end, and there is a painful discoloration over the whole surface of sensation, as though from the pricking of a needle.

div.head: On the sea-stingray
div.p: In those bitten by the sea-stingray, there occur at once severe pains, hard to master, continual spasms, distress, weakness, and disturbance of the mind; after this, loss of voice and dimming of the eyes; and the wounded place itself turns livid and black all around, and the nearby parts also become insensible to the touch; and when one wipes it, a black, thick, foul-smelling discharge issues from it.

div.head: On the shrew
div.p: In those bitten by the shrew, an inflammation forms in a circle about the site of the bite, and a black blister rises, full of a watery discharge; and everything nearby turns livid. When the blister bursts, a spreading sore takes hold, similar to that from creeping ulcers; along with these there follow griping about the intestines, difficulty in urination, and an outbreak of cold sweat.

div.head: On the viper
div.p: In those bitten by a viper, the body swells and, over a considerable area, becomes dry, taking on a whitish color; a discharge issues from the wound, at first somewhat oily, afterward bloody; blisters rise up, as in burns; and a spreading sore takes hold, advancing over everything nearby, not only on the surface but deep within as well; the gums also bleed, and an inflammation forms about the liver; griping and bilious vomiting follow; and there is also trembling, torpor, difficulty in urination, and a cold sweat all around.

div.head: On the scytale and the amphisbaena
div.p: Similar effects also occur in those bitten by the creature called the scytale, or the amphisbaena; nearly all the same remedies help. For this reason this kind has received no separate description, nor was it thought to deserve one.

div.head: On the dryinos
div.p: In those bitten by the dryinos, severe pains set in, together with blistering in the affected part, where also a watery discharge pours out; heart-sickness and griping follow as well.

div.head: On the haimorrhous
div.p: In those bitten by the haimorrhous, severe pains set in; the pores of the skin become altogether short and narrow, from the continual pains; from the bite there is a great discharge of blood; and if there is a scar anywhere on the whole body, it breaks open and bleeds; the stools too come out bloody, and the blood that is discharged is clotted; coughing, they bring up blood from the lung, and in the end they die, bleeding out beyond help.

div.head: On the dipsas
div.p: In those bitten by the dipsas, an unbearable burning heat arises, together with a thirst so intense that it is unquenchable and unceasing, and they gulp down drink greedily. Yet they come to the same state as one who has not drunk at all; and a condition of the whole frame follows resembling that of the dropsical, on account of the continual intake of drink. Hence the dipsas is also called ‘the storm’ and ‘the burning one.’

div.head: On the hydros
div.p: In those bitten by the hydros, the wound widens and grows large, turning livid; and from it issues a discharge, black, copious, and foul-smelling, such as comes from a spreading sore.

div.head: On the kenchros
div.p: In those bitten by the kenchros, the bite resembles that of the viper, but putrefaction follows; the flesh, having first swollen, wastes away round about, as in dropsy; the victims fall into a stupor and are prone to lethargy. Erasistratus says that in these cases the liver, the bladder, and the colon are affected; for when such patients have been dissected, these parts are found to be in some way corrupted.

div.head: On the cerastes
div.p: In those bitten by the cerastes, the place swells with hardness and blistering; from the bite there flows a discharge, at times black, at times pale-yellow; the whole constitution takes on a jaundiced hue; the genitals become distended; the mind is deranged, and a dimming of the eyes follows; and in the end the victim dies, convulsed by tetanus.

div.head: On the aspis
div.p: In those bitten by the aspis, the bite appears quite small, like the prick of a needle, without any swelling; only a little blood, dark and scant, drips out; a swift dimming of the eyes sets in, and a pain of many kinds spreads through the whole body — altogether light, and, strange to say, not without a certain pleasure; whence Nicander has well said: “without travail the man perishes.” The complexion becomes fixed and pale-green, with slight heart-sickness; the face is drawn back again and again; the eyelids move as though insensible, as in sleep; and death overtakes such a one along with these signs, not delaying beyond the third day.

div.head: On the basiliskos
div.p: Erasistratus, in the work called ‘On Powers and Deadly Things,’ says this in so many words about the creature called the basiliskos: ‘when the basiliskos bites, the wound takes on a golden hue.’ Such, then, are the signs that attend most of the venomous creatures. Passing now to the treatment, we shall set out first, as far as we are able, what is common to the treatment of them all.

div.head: The common treatment for venomous bites
div.p: For every wound from a venomous creature, sucking with the mouth is fitting; but he who sucks the wound should not be fasting, but should have taken food and rinsed his mouth with wine; then, holding a little oil in his mouth, let him perform the sucking in this way. The place itself should be fomented with a sponge, and afterward scarified; the incisions should be made rather deep, so as to draw the matter up from below; stripping away the flesh and excision help more abundantly than mere scarification, for these bring their own particular benefits: first, that the venom is lifted out from the place; second, that whatever has already made its way inward is expelled together with the copious flow of blood. But if the place will not allow the flesh to be stripped away, cupping-glasses should be applied with a great deal of flame. Concerning cauterization we have already spoken in the case of those bitten by a rabid animal. And if the bitten part lends itself readily to amputation, this should be done without hesitation, especially in the case of every venomous creature, as with the aspis, the cerastes, and the like. As remedies more fitting than those already mentioned, poultices deserve mention: one should apply the ash of the vine-cutting or of the fig-tree, kneaded with dripping lye, sharp fish-sauce, or salted fish; leeks, onions, and garlic, sometimes ground fine and applied as a plaster, sometimes burnt and applied to the bites; and the young of birds, split open while still very warm and wrapped about the wounded place — some have used these for a supposed sympathetic effect, though the reasoning is ready to hand: birds are by nature hot, and so, having swallowed the notable venom, they waste away from it, consuming even the driest of seeds; sometimes they even dissolve sand and stones by swallowing them; and so, in keeping with the creature’s own heat, the breath drawn from the bitten part carries the venom out along with it.

We know of something of this kind done in Egypt: whenever the Egyptians harvest the grain, they keep ready a pot of pitch, with a wasp’s nest attached to the pot. At that season they are most afraid of the creatures, both because of the time of year and because the animals lie hidden among the furrows of the fields, concealed both by the season and by the thickness of the vegetation of the land; and Egypt bears in its plains many venomous creatures more dangerous than most. So when someone is bitten on the foot or some other part, those nearby quickly throw the wasp’s nest into the pot of pitch, wind it once or twice about the forearm or the shin, a little above the bite, and two men standing by bind it tightly, and, cutting into the place through the encircling band, pour on the pitch; and when it seems to have done enough, they remove the band, and apply a poultice of onions and the other remedies already mentioned. Apart from these, warm liquid pitch mixed with fine, warmed salt is a diligent help, being kept fresh by frequent renewal; cedar-resin serves likewise, as do goats’ dung boiled in wine; a hot vinegar fomentation also assists them, and calamint boiled in urine and sea-water, or in vinegar-brine. There are also very sharp and very hot plasters able to draw out the venom, hold it, and disperse it, made with salt or soda and mustard, or with kagchrys, as shall be said next.

Not without reason does Erasistratus find fault with those who have written down powers unknown to actual use, such as the bile of the elephant and of the crocodile, and the blood and eggs of the tortoise, and the like; for such writers seem to have handed down some tradition of helpful things, but they have only deceived their readers by these very claims — such remedies could not easily be found except by royal authority, nor have they been tested by sufficient observation to warrant confidence. What is generally useful and easily obtained should instead be pointed out, remedies able to serve in every case and in all those bitten by venomous creatures. Chicory, then, and heath, and milk-vetch, drunk with vinegar, help all who have been bitten by venomous beasts; likewise bitumen, and the green balls of the plane-tree, boiled in mixed wine, and a decoction of Christ’s-thorn; and the root of aristolochia and of eryngo; and cooked bay-berries, eaten; pepper, chewed rather freely; rue, dill, and cyclamen; the tender shoots of leek eaten alone with bread, or garlic, or onions, and the sharpest salted fish; and a decoction of marjoram drunk with wine; and the juice of fennel, pennyroyal, calamint, and leeks, sipped down with honey. These, then, are from plants that grow; but certain things taken from animals are also usefully employed — the brains of cocks, eaten; the rennet of a hare, drunk with wine; and castoreum likewise. It is also said that the testicles of the sea-turtle, taken, are of help; and further, that a weasel reduced to a skeleton is found among the things spoken of — first split open entirely, its inner parts removed, and then reduced to a skeleton — and two drachms of this are drunk with wine.

So many, then, are the simple remedies commonly applied. Purging through the bowels is also fitting for those bitten by venomous beasts, together with the inducing of sweat and the copious passing of urine; and prepared draughts have also been handed down, promising newer forms of help, such as: opium and myrrh, an obol of each, and pepper, two obols — these should be taken up with honey, and given in the amount of an Egyptian bean, with wine. Likewise the seed of wild rue, black cumin, Ethiopian cumin, galbanum, and aristolochia — all these, ground fine and kneaded with the juice of rocket, are formed into pellets of a drachm’s weight; a half-cotyle of these should be given with wine. So much, then, for the remedies of common benefit; let us next speak of what is peculiar to each of the venomous creatures in turn.

div.head: On the treatment of those stung by wasps and bees
div.p: In the account of the signs we set out nothing regarding wasps and bees, for they were plain to all, and their sting carries no distinctive mark that calls for special notice; but in the matter of treatment it is not out of place to mention them as well. For the stings of wasps and bees, mallow applied as a poultice is fitting, and barley-meal with vinegar, and fig-tree sap dripped into the stings, and fomentation with brine or sea-water.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by phalangia
div.p: For those bitten by phalangia, the following should be applied: fig-tree ash with fine salt, kneaded with wine; or the root of the wild pomegranate, finely ground; or aristolochia, moistened with barley-meal and vinegar; the sores should be bathed with sea-water, or with a decoction of balm, whose leaves should also be applied as a poultice. Baths should be taken quite frequently, and draughts made from these remedies should be used beforehand: the seed of southernwood, anise, aristolochia, wild chickpea, Ethiopian cumin, ground cedar-berries, plane-bark, and the seed of trefoil grass — of each of these two portions should be given, with a cotyle of wine. The fruit of the tamarisk is likewise given, as is a decoction of ground-pine and of the tender green balls of the cypress, mixed with wine. Some also say that river-crab, pressed with milk, together with celery seed added, at once relieves the trouble.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by the scolopendra
div.p: For those bitten by the scolopendra, one should apply salt finely ground with vinegar, or wild rue, to the bite; the place should be bathed with vinegar-brine, and a draught should be given of aristolochia with wine, or of wild thyme, or of calamint, or of wild rue.

div.head: On the sting of the scorpion
div.p: For those stung by a scorpion, fig-tree sap dropped into the wounds gives immediate and precise relief; the very scorpion that struck, ground fine and applied to the stung place, becomes a remedy for its own sting, by a certain sympathetic virtue, as it seems. After this, the scorpion applied ground with salt and linseed and the marshmallow herb is fitting; native sulfur, taken up in terebinth resin and thrown on as a plaster, also helps; likewise galbanum spread out in the manner of a compress, and calamint ground and applied as a poultice, and unroasted barley-groats prepared in wine, in a decoction of rue; the seed of trefoil grass, ground and thrown on, also helps. Such, then, are the local remedies. Besides these, draughts also should be used, as being most effective: two drachms of aristolochia, especially of the bark, with wine; pounded gentian; boiled pennyroyal; a small number of bay-berries, finely ground; and calamint with vinegar-and-water, which should be well boiled in the vinegar-and-water; likewise galingale with wine, or with rue in the same way; fig-tree sap; and silphium, if it is available — if not, Parthian gum-resin should be used instead. The fruit of trefoil, drunk, is also effective, as is the seed of basil; and against all these there also stands, in aid, the constant use of the bath with much sweating, and the drinking of wine mixed with water.

div.head: On the treatment of those struck by the sea-stingray
div.p: For those struck by the sea-stingray, all the same treatment is fitting that we shall shortly describe for those bitten by vipers.

div.head: On the sea-dragon and the sea-scorpion
div.p: Particular wounds also occur from the sea-dragon and from sea-scorpions, bringing severe pains, and, though rarely, spreading sores as well. For their wounds, a draught of wormwood or of sage is fitting, or of sulfur ground with vinegar; and the creatures themselves, split open and applied to the wounds, heal the very wounds they made.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by the shrew
div.p: For those bitten by a shrew, a compress of galbanum applied over the bite is helpful, as is this remedy ground fine with vinegar, and barley-meal applied as a poultice with vinegar-and-honey; and the very shrew that bit, split open and applied, is an antidote for its own bite, as are the boiled seeds of the sweet pomegranate, applied as a poultice, and boiled leeks applied as a poultice, and pounded garlic, and fomentation with hot brine. Such are the local remedies. Given as a draught, boiled southernwood helps, administered afterward with wine; wild thyme, galbanum, and rocket dissolved in wine; the tender green balls of the cypress with vinegar; cyclamen with vinegar-and-honey; pellitory with wine; and the root of the chameleon-thistle herb. Some also record that the shrew itself, ground fine, is given as a draught for its own wound; having found this account recorded elsewhere, we thought it worth noting only in passing. Some say that the one bitten does not ulcerate unless the shrew happens to be pregnant — in which case, they say, this remedy helps.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by the viper
div.p: For those bitten by a viper, goats’ dung, applied with wine, gives ready help, and laurel likewise; southernwood and galbanum thrown on in place of a compress; fresh oregano applied loosely; and the young of birds, split open and applied at once; also vetch-meal kneaded with wine; radish bark, pounded hard until very fine; roasted squill and chamomile, ground fine; and unroasted barley-groats prepared with vinegar-and-honey, the place having first been fomented with warm water. These are applied locally. Bramble with wine also benefits those bitten by vipers; some relate that fine-leaved alkanet helps; a hare’s rennet, about three obols, is also drunk in wine, as is the juice of leek, about a half-cotyle, in unmixed wine; and the juice of balm-leaves, and wild rue — these should be given as a draught in wine; and the constant drinking of wine itself, garlic and onions eaten, tender leeks, and the sharpest, choicest salted fish. Such are the simple remedies. And the compound drug of good repute for those bitten by vipers is this: myrrh, castoreum, pepper, and realgar, one ounce of each, and half an oxybaphon of dill-seed — grind these in sweet Cretan wine, or in some other choice wine. Erasistratus, in his work On Powers, has recorded several other things able to help those bitten by vipers; the most approved of these are: the brains of birds, drunk with wine; an oxybaphon of the seed of cultivated cabbage, ground fine and drunk with wine; and it is good to dip the finger in liquid pitch and then drink it rinsed off in wine. Such, then, are the remedies for those bitten by vipers.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by the amphisbaena
div.p: Regarding the amphisbaena we have already mentioned, in the section on local remedies, how the one struck by it is helped, in the same way, by the remedies prescribed for vipers.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by the dryinos
div.p: For those struck by the dryinos, aristolochia drunk with wine is fitting, as is trefoil grass; asphodel root, taken in like manner; the fruit of every kind of oak, drunk; and the roots of the holm-oak, pounded and applied locally as a poultice, give relief.

div.head: On the treatment of those bitten by the haimorrhous and the dipsas
div.p: The bites of the haimorrhous and the dipsas have, in most of the earlier accounts, been declared beyond help, as incurable; hence there is also a lack of remedies specifically beneficial against the dipsas as such. One must nonetheless try the common remedies: scarification should be resorted to at once, and cauterization performed, and, if the place allows, amputation; then the application of sharp poultices, of which we have often spoken; sharp, pungent foods are also known to be useful, especially those made from salted fish; the drinking of unmixed wine and the bath are of benefit. These should be taken repeatedly, at short intervals, before the form of the disease has fully set in; but once it has once appeared, no help whatever comes from the physicians’ assistance. For the haimorrhous the same remedies apply, and besides these, whatever belongs to the common remedies — scarification, cauterization, sharp foods, and the drinking of unmixed wine, and all that we have prescribed for the dipsas; further, the boiled leaves of the vine, ground fine with honey.

div.head: On those bitten by the hydros
div.p: For those bitten by the hydros, oregano ground and kneaded with water is fitting, or lye mixed into oil, or the bark or root of aristolochia finely ground, and barley-meal dissolved in water with honey; a draught is also given of two drachms of aristolochia in two cups of vinegar-and-water; or the juice of horehound, or a decoction of either, with wine; and fresh honeycomb administered with vinegar.

div.head: On those bitten by the kenchridion
div.p: For those bitten by the kenchridion, the fruit of lettuce applied as a poultice with flaxseed is helpful, as is savory, and wild rue, and wild thyme ground with asphodel; given at once as a draught, two portions of centaury root with three cups of wine, or aristolochia root likewise; cress and gentian in the same way.

div.head: On those bitten by the cerastes
div.p: For those bitten by the cerastes and by the aspis, swift amputation is the surest defense; the bitten part should therefore be cut off without delay, or the flesh of the bitten parts and those nearby should be stripped away at once, and the remaining parts then dried out with cauterizing irons; for the venom of these creatures is of the same kind as that of the basiliskos.

div.head: On those bitten by the aspis
div.p: For those bitten by the aspis, the same remedies should be applied as for those bitten by the cerastes, as written above; for just as the blood of an ox curdles most sharply the blood and breath within the arteries, so does the venom of these creatures act, as does that of the basiliskos.

div.head: On those bitten by the basiliskos
div.p: For those bitten by the basiliskos, as Erasistratus says, one ounce of castoreum, drunk with wine, is helpful; likewise the sap of the poppy. Such, then, is the manner of the theriac.
